Newly hatched blue marlin larvae measure just 0.3 cm [Lb = 0.3 cm] in lower-jaw-to-fork length, a diminutive size that reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development during the early endotrophic phase. Following chorion rupture, the prolarvae emerge with a prominent yolk sac, sustaining them until the trophic switch to exogenous feeding. During this initial stage, the water temperature in spawning grounds in the western North Atlantic typically hovers near 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a thermal regime that profoundly influences developmental rates. At this temperature, the interval between syngamy and eclosion is brief, with hatching occurring approximately 7 days [ab = approximately 7 days] after at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] fertilization. The yolk-sac larva then rapidly exhausts its endogenous reserves as it transitions toward first prey capture, a critical period during which mouth gape opening and retinal differentiation must coincide with the availability of suitable planktonic prey. Mortality during this phase is extreme, as the tiny 0.3 cm [Lb = 0.3 cm] body length renders the larva vulnerable to a wide array of pelagic predators. Those that survive the early larval bottleneck begin exogenous nutrition, marking the onset of a rapid growth trajectory that will eventually transform the planktonic ichthyoplankton into a formidable apex predator.

Sexual maturation in Atlantic blue marlin is not reached until individuals achieve a lower-jaw-to-fork length of approximately 150 cm [Lp = approximately 150 cm], a size threshold that signals the onset of gonadal recrudescence and gametogenesis. Longitudinal mark-recapture studies have indicated that this milestone is attained roughly 730 days after hatching under the prevailing thermal conditions of the subtropical Atlantic, where surface waters average 28 °C [T = 28 °C], translating to an age at first reproduction of two years after hatching [tR = two years after hatching]. This relatively rapid maturation schedule, compared to other large pelagic teleosts such as tunas, likely reflects the species' early reproductive strategy to offset high natural mortality among juveniles. Upon reaching the 150 cm [Lp = 150 cm] LJFL, the HPG axis becomes activated, initiating vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Spawning is broadcast, with gamete release occurring in open water, and fecundity scales positively with female body size. The attainment of the pubertal length of 150 cm [Lp = 150 cm] thus marks a critical life-history transition, after which energy that previously fueled somatic growth begins to be partitioned toward reproductive effort.

Reproductive output in female Atlantic blue marlin increases substantially with length, as demonstrated by fecundity estimates at two key body sizes. At a LJFL of 277 cm, daily egg production at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] reaches approximately 9,863 ova per day , a considerable number that reflects the capacity for iterative spawning across a protracted breeding season. By the time a female reaches 290 cm, this rate climbs to about 18,630 ova per day , nearly doubling the reproductive potential over a modest 13 cm increase in at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]length. Both estimates were derived from gravid females captured during the peak spawning months in the Gulf of Mexico under comparable thermal conditions of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], with batch fecundity calculated via the hydrated oocyte method. This steep increase in daily egg production with female size underscores the strong size-dependence of reproductive success in makairids. Larger females not only produce more oocytes per spawning event but also likely spawn more frequently across the season, thereby magnifying their contribution to the next generation. The reproductive strategy of blue marlin is thus one of high, indeterminate fecundity, typical of iteroparous pelagic spawners.

The ultimate body size attained by Atlantic blue marlin places it among the largest of the istiophorid billfishes. Maximum recorded adult wet weight reaches 818,000 grams (818000 grams) [Wwi = 818000 grams], a massive body mass that corresponds to a lower-jaw-to-fork length of approximately 400 cm [Li = approximately 400 cm]. This asymptotic size is achieved only after decades of growth, with the oldest known individuals approaching a maximum lifespan of 10,950 days at 28 °C [T = 28 °C] or roughly 30 years after hatching [am = roughly 30 years after hatching]. The ultimate length of 400 cm [Li = 400 cm] LJFL enables the species to dominate pelagic food webs, preying upon tunas, squid, and other large nekton. Comparative analysis with related species such as the Indo-Pacific blue marlin suggests that these extreme dimensions are supported by a warm-bodied physiology that facilitates sustained swimming speeds and efficient prey capture. The attainment of 818,000 grams (818000 grams) [Wwi = 818000 grams] requires decades of nearly continuous feeding, with growth rates slowing considerably after the onset of sexual maturity as energy is diverted toward reproduction rather than further somatic increase.

In the context of the species' life-history, the maximum longevity of 30 years [am = 30 years] represents a trade-off between high investment in early reproduction and the risk of senescence-related mortality in older individuals at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Under the thermal regime of subtropical spawning grounds at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], blue marlin that surpass the 277 cm LJFL threshold continue to exhibit robust reproductive capacity, as evidenced by the daily egg production rates of 9,863 ova per day  observed in females of that size. By contrast, individuals reaching the ultimate size of 400 cm [Li = 400 cm] are rarely encountered, suggesting that only a tiny fraction of the population survives to achieve the maximum wet weight of 818,000 grams (818000 grams) [Wwi = 818000 grams] and the full potential lifespan of three decades (30 years) [am = 30 years] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. These data collectively paint a picture of a species that grows rapidly, matures early at 150 cm [Lp = 150 cm] LJFL, and invests heavily in high, sustained fecundity, yet faces intense mortality pressures that limit the number of individuals reaching the upper extremes of size and age. The interplay between thermal regime, growth rate, and reproductive output thus governs the demography of this iconic pelagic top predator.
